newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, on his feet again, seeks new harmony.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, on his feet again, seeks new harmony.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin, back on his feet on Thursday two days after massive heart surgery, issued a decree from his Moscow hospital ward aimed at setting a tone of "accord and reconciliation" for Russia.

As the 65-year-old Russian leader was recovering from a quintuple heart bypass operation, thousands of Communists carried red banners through Moscow and other Russian cities to mark the 79th anniversary of the Bolshevik revolution.
"The revolution of 1917 dramatically changed the destiny of our country," Yeltsin said in the decree.
"Keen not to allow confrontation in the future, in the interests of unity...I declare the November 7 holiday to be the Day of Accord and Reconciliation."

Yeltsin hopes Tuesday's surgery, intended to improve the flow of blood to his heart, will energize his lacklustre presidency and put in place the political and economic reforms he believes are needed to block a return to the communist past.
In an appeal to the nation, issued through his press office, he called for unity: "We are one nation. We have one fate, one future. And we are all from the same past."

But when Yeltsin leaves the Cardiology Research Centre in a western suburb of Moscow -- doctors advised him to stay another 24 hours -- he will face a restive population fed up with late salaries and pensions and fearful of a future bare of the sausage-and-vodka certainties of the Soviet past.
"On the one hand we're celebrating a holiday," a Communist marcher told Russian television: "On the other, it's a protest."
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, Yeltsin's main opponent in presidential elections earlier this year and attending a rally in central Moscow, said Russia was "on the edge of a precipice".

"There are two possibilities -- either total chaos leading to the next dictatorship and bloody struggle, or labour must unite...to establish a normal life," he told the communist faithful, marching under portraits of Vladimir Lenin, founder of the Soviet state.
But if the continuing barrage of optimistic medical bulletins issued by the Kremlin is to be believed, Yeltsin's political foes will find their sparring partner reinvigorated.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky, in his latest report, told reporters Yeltsin was recovering normally and said he met Anatoly Chubais, presidential chief of staff, for 15 minutes.
"The patient is active, can sit and stand up, walks in his ward," he said, quoting doctors who discussed Yeltsin's progress for 90 minutes on Thursday morning after he had been examined.
Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who was a consultant at the operation, said Yeltsin could be back at home in two to three weeks.

He said the president was recovering rapidly and would become a "new man". "You're going to see a vigorous leader," he said. But it would be several weeks before Yeltsin would be able to work at full strength.

The Houston, Texas doctor, who performed the world's first successful bypass in 1964, also quelled speculation over Yeltsin's alleged passion for vodka, saying he had examined his liver and seen no evidence of heavy drinking.
"He's not an alcoholic," DeBakey said and added that Yeltsin would soon be able to drink moderately.
But he said Yeltsin would be told to keep to the low-fat diet he had been on for over a month, for the rest of his life.
He called Yeltsin a motivated patient but said many bypass patients abandoned special diets and regimes as soon as they felt well.
